citation: Technology and Family Literacy Case Study: SPICE. (2012). Digital Promise. https://www.digitalpromise.org
title: Blend online learning with human support rather than offering purely online or purely face-to-face learning for adults
description: The article cites a 2009 Department of Education analysis finding that "adult learners achieve the best learning outcomes in a blended environment of online and face-to-face learning (versus only online or only face-to-face)." target_learning_goals: adult basic education and family literacy outcomes

A districtwide strategic plan
Ability to braid multiple funding streams

Children with disabilities in inclusive classrooms

article_title: Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth
citation: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text.
title: Blind, source-symmetric expert verification protocol for evaluating qualitative coding without a gold standard
description: A transferable evaluation protocol in which an independent domain expert judges anonymized pairwise comparisons of code sets without knowing which source produced which, treating human and machine sources symmetrically. The verifier "selects one of four responses: Set 1 preferred, Set 2 preferred, Both adequate, or Neither adequate", with position randomized. In this study the protocol comprised 855 stratified pairs: 555 Human vs. LLM, 210 LLM vs. LLM, 85 Human vs. Human, and 5 code supplement pairs for rare codes, supporting a binomial preference test, a Bradley-Terry model, per-code endorsement rates, and tie rates.
requirements: A verifier with domain expertise who was not involved in the original coding and has no knowledge of which sources produced which annotations.
A stratified sample large enough that each comparison stratum retains enough pairs for meaningful analysis, sized to the practical capacity of the single expert verifier.
constraints: Verification was limited to five focal models so each stratum retained enough pairs; models outside the focal set did not enter verification.
The study relies on a single independent verifier; a panel would provide stronger normative evidence and allow assessment of inter-verifier reliability.
target_learners: Social science and education researchers delegating qualitative coding to LLMs
Research teams making automation decisions about annotation pipelines
target_learning_goals: Evaluating coding quality without presupposing either human or machine superiority
Detecting shared bias that agreement-with-human-codings metrics cannot detect
examples: The verifier was a researcher with a doctoral degree in education, extensive educational research experience, and K-12 teaching experience, blind to source identity.
Human coders were placed under the same anonymized scrutiny as the models, which the authors call the study’s central methodological design move.
key_sources: Liu, A., Esbenshade, L., Xiao, M., Tian, V., Zhang, Z., He, K., & Sun, M. (2026). Agreement Is Not Quality: Blind Expert Verification of Human and LLM Qualitative Coding When Human Consensus Is Not Ground Truth. Preprint, no identifier printed in text. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.28890

article_title: From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs
citation: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009
title: Bloom-aligned framework for measuring educational control in LLMs
description: The framework operationalizes educational control — "the ability to preserve a task's instructional intent while shifting its cognitive demand toward specified learning objectives" — using revised Bloom's Taxonomy as an ordinal scale from Remember (1) to Create (6). It applies two matched intervention settings, general difficulty control and Bloom's control, and two metrics: Observed Cognitive Shift (OCS), the average movement along the taxonomy, and Target Zone Accuracy (TZA), precision of landing in the targeted zone. It is applied to programming tasks in computer science education to study the gap between solving tasks and adapting them for learners.
requirements: An LLM-as-a-judge cognitive-level classifier; the article uses claude-3.5-haiku, validated with Gwet's AC2 of 0.95 against human consensus on a 150-question subset
constraints: The judge is used to compare relative movement across matched intervention conditions rather than to assert that every absolute label is definitive
Bloom's Taxonomy serves as a structural proxy focused on task-level cognitive demand, not multi-turn tutoring dynamics or learner-specific adaptation
target_learners: programming learners in computer science education
target_learning_goals: aligning generated programming tasks with intended Bloom's Taxonomy cognitive levels
examples: Applied to a matched Qwen3-Next general/coder pair across 2,520 tasks from BigCodeBench, LiveCodeBench v5, and SWE-Bench-Verified, with four interventions per task under a shared template and decoding settings
key_sources: Yi Zhang & Julia Rayz. (2026). From Execution to Education: A Bloom-Aligned Framework for Measuring Educational Control in LLMs. Preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.08009

article_title: Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs
citation: Abdolali Faraji, Mohammadreza Molavi, Zohreh Rasoulkhani, Mohammadreza Tavakoli, and Gábor Kismihók. (2026). Cross-Dataset Bloom Question Classification: Supervised Models and Prompted LLMs. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.13684
title: Lightweight UI for instructor-driven Bloom classification built on the selected-questions-verbs prompt
description: A lightweight tool built on the article's best-performing prompting strategy. Instructors provide a small set of example questions per Bloom level for their context; the tool "extracts key action verbs from these examples" and uses them with the examples to construct the classification prompt. Users upload question sets in CSV/Excel and receive Bloom-level predictions in structured output. A user study with N=50 Prolific participants reported low workload (NASA-TLX means: mental demand 2.32, effort 2.46, frustration 1.68) and mean SUS of 78.2 (SD 14.07).
requirements: Instructors must supply example questions per Bloom level for their specific course, topic, or learning objectives
constraints: The article notes feedback from real instructors would provide more precise insights for practical deployment, as the UI was tested with pilot users
target_learning_goals: automatic Bloom-level classification of assessment questions
examples: In the usability study, participants interacted with the UI for 10 minutes for one of their real courses and added Bloom-level examples

article_title: From Memorization to Creation: Evaluating the Cognitive Depth of LLM-Generated Educational Questions
citation: Xiaolong Wang, Zhe Zhao, Song Lai, Chaoli Zhang, Zijie Geng, Yu Tong, Ye Wei, and Qingsong Wen. 2026. From Memorization to Creation: Evaluating the Cognitive Depth of LLM-Generated Educational Questions. Proceedings of the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining V.1 (KDD '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3770854.3785686
title: Bloom-driven cognitive-leap evaluation framework with CogShift, category consistency, and knowledge coverage metrics
description: A Bloom's-Taxonomy-driven framework for evaluating LLM-generated educational questions that pivots "from a knowledge-point perspective to a cognitive-leap paradigm". It combines usability filtering (unique, readable, answerable via majority voting across GPT evaluators), category consistency (CatCons), knowledge coverage (KnowCov), and a Cognitive Shift Score (CogShift) that weights mismatches by the ordinal distance between original and generated Bloom levels, classifying shifts as leap, regression, or drift. The framework was applied to 20,700 questions across six LLMs and three domains.

Annotated Bloom levels for source questions
Automated evaluation models with majority voting and low-agreement cases discarded (Krippendorff's alpha < 0.7)
constraints: Bloom-level agreement between the automatic rubric and expert annotations is modest at 46.58%, so fine-grained estimation of cognitive depth remains an open problem
The K-12 math evaluation fixes the Bloom level to 'apply', limiting cognitive-shift analysis in that domain
target_learning_goals: generating questions that stimulate higher-order thinking
aligning question cognitive depth with learners' cognitive stages
preserving target knowledge units in generated questions
examples: Applied to six LLMs (GLM4-9B-Chat, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Baichuan2-7B-Chat, InternLM3-8B-Instruct, Meta-LLaMA3-8B-Instruct-Chinese, Spark3.5-Max) on computer science, K-12 math, and social-science question sets

article_title: What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries
citation: Germana Bertoli, Ilaria Amelia Caggiano, Francesca Lagioia, Riccardo Rovatti, Giovanni Sartor, Emiliano Troisi. (2025). What out-of-the-box LLMs can(t) do in law? A Turing test in Italian exams for lawyers, judges and notaries. https://github.com/SSIGPRO/LLMs-in-legal-professions
title: Blind Turing-test evaluation protocol for LLM legal exam papers
description: An evaluation design in which LLM-generated and human exam papers are formatted identically and anonymously assessed by expert examiners using official criteria. Three domain experts who had served on national board committees each evaluated five uniformly formatted papers with no indication of authorship. "we employed highly skilled professionals with direct experience in national boards as evaluators, through a 'Turing Test' approach, capturing qualitative nuances, often missed by automated metrics." The human benchmark was the highest-scoring candidate's real exam paper, digitised via OCR and manually verified.
requirements: Expert evaluators with direct national-board examination experience
Uniform formatting making LLM and human papers visually indistinguishable
Official assessment grids from the Italian Ministry of Justice
constraints: Limited number of exam papers and a small pool of three expert evaluators, constraining statistical generalisation
LLMs had internet access while human candidates were restricted to limited legal materials
Situated within the Italian legal system
target_learning_goals: assessing LLM legal competence under authentic professional examination conditions
examples: Prompts used a simple uniform structure with a persona declaration, task description, verbatim exam question, and instructions; case-law references were removed from all documents to ensure uniformity.

article_title: Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval
citation: Monica S. Birnbaum, Nate Kornell, Elizabeth Ligon Bjork, & Robert A. Bjork. (2013). Why interleaving enhances inductive learning: The roles of discrimination and retrieval. Memory & Cognition, 41, 392–402. https://doi.org/10.3758/s13421-012-0272-7
title: Dual-process framework: blocking supports within-category similarity processing, interleaving supports between-category difference processing
description: The authors adopt a conceptual framework in which "blocking facilitates processing of similarities within a category, whereas interleaving facilitates processing of differences between categories". Because categories are defined by both similarities and differences, both processes matter, and the optimal schedule depends on which is harder for the given materials. The framework is offered to reconcile apparently divergent prior findings that blocking sometimes helped.
requirements: Learners must process both within-category similarities and between-category differences for complete category learning
constraints: The authors speculate tentatively that prior blocking benefits arose when materials made identifying similarities difficult, noting the prior studies used artificial categories, more practice trials, and fewer categories
target_learning_goals: category learning balancing similarity and difference processing
examples: Zulkiply and Burt found blocking more effective for highly discriminable categories and interleaving critical for low-discriminability categories, which the authors cite as supporting the framework

article_title: Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases
citation: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z
title: Three forms of noticing required for learning to facilitate productive discussion
description: Building on Gibson's perceptual learning theory, the article proposes three forms of noticing for teachers developing discussion facilitation. "First is increased differentiation with respect to the structure and features of student talk, including both what is present and what is missing." Second, differentiation of the features and dimensions of teachers' response moves; third, identification and refinement of one's values and commitments and of alignment between a discussion and those values. The intervention was designed around these three areas.
requirements: Requires teachers to encounter varied discussion examples that make features of student talk, teacher moves, and values contrasts salient
constraints: The matching-problem analogy is acknowledged as a simplification; discussion also occurs in social and cultural contexts shaped by values and relational histories the analogy does not capture
target_learning_goals: noticing features of productive classroom discussion
differentiating talk moves such as revoicing
refining values and commitments about discussion
examples: The contrasting cases activity was designed so that ranking and principle generation engaged all three areas of development

article_title: Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases
citation: Blair, K. P., Banes, L. C., & Martin, L. (2024). Fostering noticing of classroom discussion features through analysis of contrasting cases. Instructional Science, 52:417–452. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11251-024-09661-z
title: Contrasting cases with a synthesis (inventing principles) task to develop perceptual differentiation of discussion features
description: The instructional approach uses "juxtaposed examples that are chosen to highlight distinctive features or relationships", with most features held constant so key differences stand out. Learners synthesize across multiple cases by inventing guiding principles, in line with Schwartz and Martin's (2004) approach, so that differentiation of stimuli and of principles reinforce each other and support transfer. The activity prepares learners for an expert recap, creating "a time-for-telling".
requirements: Cases must be carefully chosen so pairwise comparisons isolate particular features; a synthesis task across the cases; a subsequent expert discussion and lecture to consolidate what was noticed
constraints: The authors used constructed transcripts rather than video because natural classroom variability makes tight video contrasts challenging; chosen features are a subset known to be important, not exhaustive
target_learning_goals: noticing present and absent discussion features

citation: Seyyed Kazem Banihashem, Dragan Gašević, Omid Noroozi, Halszka Jarodzka, Desiree Joosten-ten Brinke, Hendrik Drachsler. (2025). Optimizing Formative Assessment with Learning Analytics. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543251370753
title: Black and Wiliam's (2009) model of formative assessment as the review's organizing framework: three agents crossing three key processes
description: The review adopts Black and Wiliam's (2009) model, in which formative assessment is 'assessment for learning' undertaken by three agents — teachers, peers, and learners — across three processes: where the learner is going, where the learner is now, and how to get there. title: Blend teacher autonomy support with provision of structure rather than treating them as opposites
description: The article's central recommendation is that teachers should blend autonomy support and provision of structure, because the two constructs reinforce each other and both elevate student outcomes. The authors state: "Our findings suggest blending autonomy support and structure for optimal growth of students and teachers." The recommendation rests on the pooled positive correlation between the constructs and their independent associations with student motivation, engagement, and need satisfaction, and on evidence that students benefit most when structure is provided in an autonomy-supportive rather than controlling manner.
requirements: Teachers must distinguish structure from control, since control undermines motivation while structure supports competence
constraints: The relationship between the two constructs was moderated by data collection method and school level; teacher-report studies sometimes showed negative correlations
examples: The review found 86 of 94 studies described the two constructs as independent but positively related aspects of teachers' instructional approaches

article_title: Communications and discussions. Inexpert Binet examiners and their limitations.
citation: E. A. Doll. (1912). Inexpert Binet Examiners and Their Limitations. The Journal of Educational Psychology. https://www.jstor.org
title: Fault for misdiagnosis with the Binet tests lies with inexpert examiners, not with the tests themselves
description: Responding to criticism of the Binet tests at the Fourth International Congress on School Hygiene, the author argues it is more just to attack inexpert examiners who do only mechanical Binet testing than to condemn the tests. The analogy is drawn to inexperienced nurses who incorrectly interpret thermometric readings, where blame falls on the nurse and not the thermometer. The principle holds that determining normality or abnormality requires expertise beyond Binet testing itself.

constraints: The principle does not extend to defending reports drawn by examiners whose knowledge and experience do not warrant the conclusions they attempt.

target_learning_goals: accurate diagnosis of children's intellectual normality or abnormality
examples: The article compares inexpert Binet examiners to "many inexperienced nurses incorrectly interpret thermometric readings, although in such cases we blame the nurse and not the thermometer".

title: Blended video-based proportional reasoning math course built in Articulate 360 with segmented videos, worked examples, and standardized UX interface

This study applies LFM to quantitative chemistry instruction.

examples: The study exposed the experimental group to mastery learning for two weeks and compared post-test outcomes against a conventionally taught control group

description: The study's treatment instrument was an online reading comprehension exercise based on the same 770-word text as the post-test, delivered via Blackboard. Two versions were created: one with elaborative feedback providing additional guidance and support, and one with knowledge of response feedback that simply informed the reader whether their response was correct or incorrect. Both were answer until correct feedback allowing multiple attempts per question.
requirements: Learner familiarity with the Blackboard learning management system to minimise access difficulties
examples: Following an incorrect response to Question 11, the elaborative feedback prompted re-reading of paragraph 3 with guiding questions, whereas the knowledge of response feedback stated simply Incorrect.

article_title: The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy
citation: Sasan Baleghizadeh and Atieh Masoun. (2013). The Effect of Self-Assessment on EFL Learners' Self-Efficacy. TESL Canada Journal/Revue TESL du Canada, Volume 31, Issue 1. https://teslcanadajournal.ca
title: Ten-item self-assessment questionnaire adapted from Blanche and Merino (1989)
description: The treatment instrument was a self-assessment questionnaire adapted from Blanche and Merino (1989) in which "students are asked to identify classroom topics (whether grammatical, functional, or lexical) they consider important", rate their importance and their ability to learn them on 5-item scales, list new vocabulary, give a general evaluation of learning, and describe weaknesses and desired changes to study habits. Experimental-group students completed it biweekly for about 30-35 minutes at the end of each unit, three times over a seven-week course, without receiving any score.
requirements: Completed on a formative, ungraded basis so students do not feel compelled to raise scores to please the instructor
constraints: Administered only to the experimental group, three times over a seven-week course, with adult intermediate EFL learners
target_learners: adult intermediate EFL learners at a language institute
target_learning_goals: self-assessment of topics, vocabulary, and learning gains in an EFL course
examples: The full 10-item instrument is printed in Appendix A, including rating scales from not at all to thoroughly/extremely

citation: Hussein El-ghamry Mohammad Hussein. (2016). The Effect of Blackboard Collaborate-Based Instruction on Pre-service Teachers' Achievement in the EFL Teaching Methods Course at Faculties of Education for Girls. English Language Teaching, 9(3). https://doi.org/10.5539/elt.v9n3p49
title: Blackboard Collaborate web conferencing system with ten interface components
description: Blackboard Collaborate (previously known as Elluminate Live) is defined in the study as "a web conferencing system which allows participants (teachers and students) to communicate synchronously and asynchronously, view presentations or videos, interact with other participants, and engage with resources in work groups". The article details ten components, including the Title Bar, Menu Bar, Audio and Video Panel, Participants Panel, Chat Panel, Collaboration Toolbar, and Content Area, and used it as the delivery platform for the experimental group's teaching methods course.
requirements: Participants need adequate computer specifications, proper technical support, and training in different kinds of software, per the article's discussion of the need for high end technology
constraints: The article notes drawbacks: lack of learner awareness, the need for high end technology, and frequent technical failures such as Internet connection failures mid-lesson

target_learning_goals: EFL teaching methods knowledge and skills, including lesson planning, objectives, questioning strategies, and error correction

article_title: A Pilot Study on the Comparison between Blended and F2F Learning Methods in a SQL Course
citation: Yavuzarslan, M., Olgun, H., & Yazici, S. (2019). A Pilot Study on the Comparison Between Blended and F2F Learning Methods in a SQL Course. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology. http://www.tojet.net
title: Use blended learning design to teach programming because it offers anytime access to materials and repeated practice on difficult tasks
description: The article argues that blended learning design has several advantages for computing education. It "allows users for accessing the exercises, course materials, examples and their solutions any time" so students develop deep comprehension of programming notions, and it may include activities that direct students to improve their skills by repeating difficult tasks. Students facing difficulties can use both discussion forums and F2F meetings for seeking help. The authors present this as highlighting the functionality of blended learning design in computing education.
requirements: Rich learning environments are needed to address students' different learning styles and various sources of motivations, as the article states citing Jenkins (2002)
constraints: The pilot's own two-week result favored F2F, and the authors state the time of the training should be described and organized well to allow learners to develop such skills
target_learning_goals: developing programming skills and deep comprehension of programming notions
examples: In the pilot, the blended group accessed the SQL Course platform freely for two weeks and practiced SQL statements in the W3 SQL Tryit Editor at the end of each section.

article_title: Reexamining the Effectiveness of Vocabulary Learning via Mobile Phones
citation: Haisen Zhang, Wei Song, Jack Burston. (2011). REEXAMINING THE EFFECTIVENESS OF VOCABULARY LEARNING VIA MOBILE PHONES. The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 10(3). https://www.tojet.net
title: Use mobile SMS vocabulary learning as a complement to traditional vocabulary learning within a blended approach
description: The article recommends that mobile phones "can only be used as a complement of traditional vocabulary learning such as use of vocabulary books and dictionaries, as well as context-based vocabulary learning." Because SMS's disadvantages minimized long-term effects, blending the novel approach with traditional approaches may offset their respective weaknesses and improve sustained retention. The authors state the question of how each approach's effectiveness can be augmented still needs further testing.
requirements: Repeated exposures to target vocabulary must be maintained for effectiveness to persist
constraints: The innate weaknesses of SMS technology reduce effective application, especially lack of multiple ways of interaction between learner and technology
target_learners: Chinese university EFL students preparing for the College English Test
target_learning_goals: Intentional English vocabulary learning and sustained retention
examples: The experimental group received 5 vocabulary items by SMS twice daily (12 pm and 5:30 pm) for 26 days via Fetion, while the control group studied the same 130-word paper list in a self-regulated manner

article_title: Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK
citation: Arwa Ahmed Abdo Qasem, Gandla Viswanathappa. (2016). Blended Learning Approach to Develop the Teachers' TPACK. Contemporary Educational Technology, 7(3), 264-276. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.sbspro.2013.09.248
title: Blended learning professional development model for teacher ICT training (12 face-to-face + 20 online sessions)
description: A flexible blended learning model in which an online platform delivers most of the curricula: face-to-face instruction comprised 12 sessions in a computer lab (project discussion, feedback, workshop, computer-assisted instruction), and online learning comprised 20 asynchronous (e-mail, discussion forum, Facebook) and synchronous (chat, video, audio conference) sessions. The program ran approximately 8 weeks, 4 days per week, totalling 32 two-hour periods, and was delivered via a web-based learning platform (https://sites.google.com/site/alearningy/). The control group received 32 classroom and computer-laboratory sessions with trainer-discussed assignments instead.
requirements: An online platform delivering the curricula with sequential navigation elements
Face-to-face computer lab sessions alongside online asynchronous and synchronous components
constraints: Evaluated with in-service science teachers in Yemen; the article notes relatively limited empirical evidence on blended learning in teacher education programs generally
examples: Participants joined the website via emailed invitations and followed weekly plans of four sessions, e.g. for Communication Skills

article_title: The Combined Impact of the Flipped Classroom, Collaborative Learning, on Students' Learning of Key Marketing Concepts
citation: Motameni, R. (2018). The Combined Impact of the Flipped Classroom, Collaborative Learning, on Students' Learning of key Marketing Concepts. Journal of University Teaching & Learning Practice, 15(3). https://ro.uow.edu.au/jutlp/vol15/iss3/4
title: Three-module conceptual framework linking Bloom's Revised Taxonomy, flipped classroom and collaborative learning
description: The article proposes a synthesised conceptual framework (Figure 2) consisting of "three interrelated and integrated modules that constitute a flipped classroom: learning processes, assessment processes and collaborative-learning processes". Module 1 covers online self-learning of key concepts, Module 2 covers quizzes, self-assessments and formal exams, and Module 3 covers higher-order collaborative work culminating in a marketing plan. Lower-order cognitive work occurs online independently while higher-order work occurs in class with peer and instructor support. The framework served as the blueprint for the study's course restructuring.
requirements: Students must complete lower-level learning and assessment modules before applying concepts in the collaborative module
target_learning_goals: learning 100 key marketing concepts, processes and strategies
higher-order thinking skills of applying, analysing, evaluating and creating
examples: Students used Cengage MKTG Online e-books, e-lectures, concept videos and flash cards in Module 1, then completed seven collaborative sessions creating a marketing plan for a Fortune 500 company in Module 3

article_title: The Influence of Blended Learning Environment on Self-Regulated and Self-Directed Learning Skills of Learners
citation: Uz, R., & Uzun, A. (2018). The influence of blended learning environment on self-regulated and self-directed learning skills of learners. European Journal of Educational Research, 7(4), 877-886. https://doi.org/10.12973/eu-jer.7.4.877
title: Design blended learning environments around learner-centered access, self-evaluation, feedback and communication opportunities
description: The article's design was based on principles from the self-regulated and self-directed learning literature: materials grouped weekly and accessible at learners' convenience, varied material types for differing learning styles, end-of-material tests with visible scores for self-evaluation, and project-based and forum communication for active participation. The authors summarize that learners could "monitor, evaluate and receive feedback on their learning" in this learner-centered environment.
requirements: The instructor must be able to use technology effectively and develop a variety of materials to meet individual differences
The instructor needs more time to give feedback as asynchronous communication opportunities increase
constraints: Designing a blended learning environment requires more time and effort than designing a traditional learning environment, and developing materials that encourage active participation is a major instructor problem
examples: The experimental environment offered presentations, videos, tests, projects and forums, with three-attempt practice questions and a Grades link showing individual success reports

article_title: The Impact of Teaching Oriental Music Using Blended Learning Approach
citation: Chamila Nishanthi Edward, David Asirvatham & Md Gapar Md Johar. (2019). The Impact of Teaching Oriental Music Using Blended Learning Approach. Malaysian Journal of Learning and Instruction, 16(1), 81-103. https://mjli.uum.edu.my
title: Blended Oriental Music course: 50% face-to-face / 50% online with 5E lesson plans on Moodle
description: The researchers designed a six-week (Grade 11) and eight-week (Grade 10) blended course proportionating "50 percent of face to face learning and 50 percent of online learning". The normal 80-minute weekly period was split into 30 minutes face-to-face instruction and 50 minutes lab instruction, with lesson exploration done through the Moodle LMS. Lesson plans followed the 5E instructional design model (Engage, Explore, Explain, Elaborate, Evaluate) and targeted competencies difficult for students, such as practical singing/playing, creative works, and performing abilities.
requirements: Requires an LMS (Moodle) with student registration and access to computers, plus supplementary audio and video materials prepared for weekly lessons
constraints: Depends on available technology infrastructure; the article notes the Moodle network reached 300 senior secondary schools with WAN connection through SchoolNet
target_learners: Grade 10 and 11 students studying Oriental Music for GCE Ordinary Level in Sri Lankan government schools
target_learning_goals: Oriental Music theory and practical competencies required at Ordinary Level
examples: Face-to-face sessions used multimedia presentations and audio video supplementary materials; online learning was done through the David's Learning Centre LMS Moodle

article_title: Is Blended e-Learning as Measured by an Achievement Test and Self-Assessment Better than Traditional Classroom Learning for Vocational High School Students?
citation: Chang, Shu, Liang, Tseng, and Hsu. (2014). Is Blended E-Learning Better than Traditional Classroom Learning for Vocational High School Students? Vol 15 | No 2 April/14. http://el.evta.gov.tw/
title: Blended e-learning activity structured across eight learning phases
description: The study organized its blended e-learning activity based on "the eight learning phases proposed by Baldwin-Evans (2006) and Bielawski and Metcalf (2005)": Prepare me, Tell me, Show me, Let me, Check me, Support me, Coach me, and Connect me. Weekly sessions combined two in-class lecture hours with one e-learning hour, plus after-class discussion board and email support. Paper-based and online practice and tests let students check their learning progress.
requirements: A syllabus emailed to students and an orientation introducing blended e-learning before the course
constraints: The sequence was traditional learning followed by e-learning, with e-learning treated as a supporting tool provided after class
target_learning_goals: electrical machinery knowledge and skills (transformer unit)
examples: Each week: traditional lecture on the textbook topic, then an online course with similar content for review, online practice and test, and discussion board or email support after class

article_title: Complementary Learning: Piloting a Blended Format for Canadian Composition Courses
citation: Stouck, J. (2019). Complementary Learning: Piloting a Blended Format for Canadian Composition Courses. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5206/cjsotl-rcacea.2019.1.7992
title: Use blended scheduling to restore one-on-one feedback and small-group workshop time lost in large composition classes
description: The principle holds that rotating part of a composition course online restructures class time so that face-to-face meetings occur in half-sized groups devoted to feedback, editing, and discussion. In this pilot, students attended two thirds of the course F2F and one third online, and the author reports that "the blended format addressed class size by allowing the one-on-one time and small workshop activities that tend to be lost with classes over 20 students." Student TEQ comments praised the smaller workshops and increased one-on-one professor contact.
requirements: Instructors must carefully review all course materials to decide which content is best covered online versus face-to-face, following the article's thoughtful-integration design process
constraints: Both instructors reported the approach does not reduce, and may even add to, instructor workload; blended teaching is not intended to enable ever-larger class sizes
examples: Two 2014 sections and one 2016 section of English 112 rotated attendance so half the class met in alternating sessions, freeing time for personal feedback, editing, and discussion.

article_title: Complementary Learning: Piloting a Blended Format for Canadian Composition Courses
citation: Stouck, J. (2019). Complementary Learning: Piloting a Blended Format for Canadian Composition Courses. The Canadian Journal for the Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, 10(1). https://doi.org/10.5206/cjsotl-rcacea.2019.1.7992
title: Blended composition course pattern: online lectures, readings, and writing exercises paired with weekly F2F feedback sessions
description: This course-level pattern splits a genre-based first-year composition course so that core content delivery and writing practice occur online while class time concentrates on discussion, workshop, and formative feedback. The blended version used "short recorded lectures, electronic readings, and frequent opportunities for online writing and feedback alongside weekly student-instructor interaction time," with recorded discussions of discipline-specific writing practices. Students absent from a session were required to view material, relate it to the textbook, and complete an online writing exercise for a nominal 2% mark.
requirements: A learning management system hosting video lectures, electronic readings, editing exercises, and an online dropbox; coordinated content, assignments, and rubrics when multiple instructors teach the format
constraints: Students were required to attend two thirds of the course F2F; the online discussion group provided was not used by students; two instructors introduced variations in timing and delivery styles
target_learning_goals: research writing, summary, analysis, persuasion, revision, and scholarly writing style
examples: English 112 control sections (2013, fully F2F) were compared with blended sections (2014 and 2016) covering the same core material, learning outcomes, assignments, and readings.

article_title: Teaching Music as a University Elective Course through e-Learning
citation: Adileh, M. (2012). Teaching music as a university elective course through e-learning. Australian Journal of Music Education, 2012(1), 71-79. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ976542
title: Combine face-to-face sessions with an online course website providing multimedia-rich materials and interaction tools
description: The study's blended condition paired weekly 1.5-hour classroom meetings with a course website offering "online lecture notes and multimedia-rich components, such as screen captures, assessment simulations, and online tutorials." Interaction tools included questions, e-mail, and web announcements; teamwork and discussions supported collaboration. This combination produced higher achievement and attitudes than FTF alone in the study.

constraints: Studied in a university elective music course with Palestinian students; the article notes some reviewed literature (e.g., Tang & Byrne, 2007) found no significant achievement difference between modes
target_learners: university students in elective music courses
target_learning_goals: knowledge of musical forms, instruments, and notation
examples: The experimental group met 1.5 hours weekly in class and accessed screen captures, assessment simulations, and online tutorials through the course website for 14 weeks

title: Researcher-developed geometry achievement test based on Bloom's taxonomy
description: An achievement test prepared by the researchers to measure sixth-grade students' performance and perception of geometrical material after treatment, including multiple-choice and written questions, with a total score of 30 marks. citation: Suprabha. K, & Subramonian, G. (2015). Blended learning approach for enhancing students learning experiences in a knowledge society. i-manager's Journal of Educational Technology, 11(4). http://www.eric.ed.gov
title: Blended learning as a student-centred combination of face-to-face and online instruction
description: The article frames blended learning as courses that "combine face-to face classroom instruction with online learning", involving a shift away from lecture-style instruction toward a more student-centred style. It is described as a mix of pedagogical approaches combining the effectiveness and socialisation opportunities of the classroom with the technological enhancements of online learning. Garrison and Vaughan's (2008) key assumptions are thoughtfully integrating face-to-face and online learning, rethinking course design to optimise student engagement, and restructuring and replacing traditional class contact hours.

A fundamental rethinking of course design to optimise student engagement
Restructuring and replacing traditional class contact hours

title: Success factors for blended learning: guidance, collective work, innovation, flexible choices, learner participation in blend choice, continuous communication, and repetition

article_title: A Comparison of Two Curricular Models of Professional Development to Increase Teacher Repertoires for Instructing Students with Autism
citation: Dille, L. (2013). A Comparison of Two Curricular Models of Professional Development to Increase Teacher Repertoires for Instructing Students with Autism. Journal of the American Academy of Special Education Professionals (JAASEP), Fall 2013. https://jaasep.org
title: Blended Model curriculum: ten lessons blending behavioral and socio-emotional approaches for teaching students with autism
description: The Blended Model curriculum was a ten-lesson professional development sequence. Foundational lessons on autism diagnosis and characteristics preceding the blended-pedagogy lessons
constraints: The article states the study's training may have been insufficiently extensive; future studies with more extensive training are recommended
target_learners: Teachers of students with autism across school-based, inclusion, preschool, early-intervention, and home-based settings
target_learning_goals: Applying a blended behavioral and socio-emotional pedagogical approach to students with mild/moderate and severe autism
examples: In the study, the Blended group's mean increase on the application measure was 18.250 points versus 9 points for the Behavioral group

citation: Said Fathy El Said Abdul Fattah. (2016). The Effectiveness of Using Blogs as an Independent Learning Tool to Develop Reading Skills for University Students. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.32. http://www.iiste.org
title: Blogs as a support for learner autonomy through responsibility, personalization, and reflection
description: Drawing on Benson's (2007) definition of learner autonomy as "the ability of learners to take charge of their own learning" and Little's (1991) account, the article presents blogs as promoting autonomy in four areas: encouraging decision making (students may post, write, delete, add or change in their own blog), giving students responsibility over one aspect of learning and its documents, enabling transfer and personalization of formally learned language, and offering opportunities to reflect on their language use and learning process. constraints: The article notes it will be difficult to leave learners alone, so blogs are proposed as the way to achieve independence
examples: The study's program made students responsible for their own reading practice outside class hours

Heterogeneous grouping arranged with attention to special students' physical and mental development

description: The article defines blended learning as "the harmonized combining of face to face and online (e-learning) environments to present the learner a large and effective learning process". The instructor and the learner have to carry through their tasks and responsibilities

title: Bloom, Raudenbush, and Weiss multilevel methodology for estimating variation in program impacts across individuals, subgroups, and sites
description: The article applies a new and innovative methodology for estimating sources of variation in program impacts (Bloom, 2012; Bloom, Raudenbush, & Weiss, 2013). It uses a two-level model with a random treatment-effect component across center groups, estimated with new capabilities in the HLM software, and tests cross-site impact variance with a Chi-Square test of the Q statistic used in meta-analysis. Crucially, it distinguishes variation in program effect estimates from variation in true program effects, accounting for estimation error.
requirements: Requires new capabilities in the HLM software to produce an unbiased estimate of the cross-site impact variance and a non-symmetric confidence interval
Requires randomized assignment within center groups and outcome data on treated and control children
constraints: Because of estimation error, variation in estimates of program effects is often many times the variation in true program effects
Cross-center variation analyses were still underway; results were to be presented at SREE
target_learners: Low-income preschool children in Head Start programs
target_learning_goals: School readiness: receptive vocabulary, early reading, oral comprehension, early numeracy, externalizing behavior, self-regulation
examples: Applied to the first follow-up year of the Head Start Impact Study, with 3,785 children in 202 center groups randomized within center group

citation: Fontenot, J., Carney, K. J., & Hansen, K. (2015). Conspicuous Strategies in Teaching Expressive Writing: A Quantitative Study Comparing Two Approaches to Process Writing. Journal of Instructional Research, 4. https://jir.gcu.edu
title: Blueprint Writing (BW) approach
description: The BW approach is a systematic process-writing intervention built around a color-coded graphic organizer for writing paragraphs called a blueprint. Per the article, it "was designed to incorporate conspicuous strategies into the explicit teaching of the writing process", stimulating oral language before writing via vocabulary-building activities and multi-sensory experiences. It adds explicit teaching of writing vocabulary, visual graphic organizers, peer-assisted learning in pre-writing and editing, three-stage editing, and authentic publishing outcomes, and was delivered to teachers in six sessions totaling 10 hours. requirements: Teacher training in the conspicuous and interactive strategies (six sessions totaling 10 hours in the study)
constraints: The study tested BW as a composite process, so which individual techniques accounted for growth could not be determined
target_learners: elementary students in inclusive sixth-grade classrooms
examples: School A teachers implemented BW for four months with sixth graders, outperforming the PW school on WIAT-II Written Expression growth

title: Blended e-learning as a complement of e-learning tools with traditional face-to-face learning

Knowledge of how to integrate face-to-face teaching methods with internet-based instruction

constraints: The article notes this is a theoretical rationale; the study could not isolate previewing as the sole cause of improvement

examples: The article cites Krathwohl (2002) and argues that previewing enables application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation during the lecture itself

title: Blended, peer-led, AI-integrated research methods curriculum with eight structured components
description: The intervention is an eight-component postgraduate research methods program: flipped self-produced video lectures, gamified weekly group article critiques, in-class study design tasks, CASP peer appraisal rounds, faculty-led roundtable discussions, online expert lectures, supplementary skill activities, and a final proposal with oral defense. The article describes "a blended, student-centered research methods program integrating flipped learning, structured peer critique, active application tasks, and regulated use of AI tools." ChatGPT was permitted to improve clarity of critiques without replacing student reasoning; the control group received traditional lectures with AI prohibited.
requirements: Faculty training, ongoing support, and dedicated preparation and feedback time, which the authors state may limit scalability in resource-constrained settings
Transparent guidelines around AI use and balanced workload
constraints: Resource-intensive to deliver
Implemented in a single postgraduate dental program with cohort-based learning and close faculty supervision
target_learning_goals: Research literacy and critical appraisal competence
Research proposal development and thesis preparedness
examples: Intervention students watched more than 50 self-produced YouTube lectures before class and completed weekly gamified group critiques of assigned articles with AI tools allowed

title: Blended simulation skills course pattern: asynchronous online theory followed by supervised hands-on practice with individual equipment and 1–1 objective assessment
description: The article's course design combines a short asynchronous online theory module with a synchronous, closely supervised simulation practice session ending in a 1–1 objective assessment. Students valued "a balanced integration of theory and practical skills" and "individual access to US equipment" rather than crowding around shared kit, and identified supportive tutors and organisational consistency as enablers of successful delivery. Supervising tutors available throughout practice
Consistent trainers and delivery across cohorts
A validated objective assessment instrument

Students requested increased simulation realism, e.g. practising explaining the procedure to simulated patients

target_learning_goals: Acquisition and objective assessment of a procedural clinical skill
examples: The 120-minute synchronous session allocated 45 minutes to theory, 45 minutes to closely supervised practice and 30 minutes to 1–1 objective assessment.

title: Bloom's-taxonomy-based ACS assessment instrument with reported reliability
description: A closed-book multiple-choice exam designed for this study to assess theoretical knowledge, divided equally into basic theoretical knowledge (100 points) and clinical case analysis (100 points). "All the questions in the test were based on Bloom's Taxonomy", with remembering (20%), understanding (30%), applying (25%), analyzing (15%), evaluating (7%), and creating (3%); the first two categories formed the basic knowledge section and the remainder the clinical case analysis section. Internal consistency of the MCQs was Cronbach's alpha 0.82, inter-rater reliability of the skill exam was Cohen's kappa 0.89, and the tools were piloted on students outside the main intervention.

Pilot testing was conducted on a small subset of same-year students who did not participate in the main intervention
constraints: The instrument was designed for this single study at one institution
examples: Skill examination reliability was evaluated using Cohen's kappa, yielding a coefficient of 0.89

article_title: A reflective learning conversation debriefing model for interprofessional simulation based education.
citation: Almomani Emad, Tobin John, Fernandes Sonia, Sullivan Jacqueline, Saadeh Omar, Mustafa Emad, Pattison Natalie, Alinier Guillaume. (2025). title: Use Bloom's Taxonomy in debriefing as a flexible guide rather than a rigid framework
description: The authors caution that the incremental, Bloom-structured questioning of models like RLC carries a rigidity risk if applied rigidly across experience levels: highly experienced participants may disengage if basic questions dominate, while novices may find advanced questions overwhelming. They therefore advise that "Bloom's Taxonomy is perhaps best used as a flexible guide rather than a rigid framework by competent debriefers", adapting questioning to individual needs while balancing group objectives.
requirements: Competent debriefers able to judge and adapt question difficulty to learners' needs
constraints: Power imbalances within groups can limit contributions from less experienced participants, affecting engagement and reasoning development
examples: The RLC model sequences questioning from basic knowledge to higher-order analysis via Bloom's Taxonomy, which the authors note may encourage participation from less experienced learners.

citation: Hsu Ming-Sung, Yeh Chun-Liang, Cheng Shih-Jung, Lin Chun-Pin. (2025). Transforming Dental Morphology Education: The Impact of Three-Dimensional Digital Simulation on Practical Skill Development. International Dental Journal. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.identj.2025.103904
title: Use a blended learning approach in which preclass digital 3D models precede, but do not replace, hands-on instruction
description: The article recommends integrating 3D digital simulation before traditional hands-on sessions rather than as a standalone method. In the trial, the experimental group received a 90-minute instructor-led digital course and self-directed practice with interactive 3D tooth models before the same plaster carving session the control group had, and students "remained neutral regarding the digital course's capacity to entirely replace hands-on instruction". The authors conclude that "A blended learning approach is recommended."
requirements: Access to 3D digital tools (exocad software and interactive 3D tooth models on mobile or desktop devices) and an instructor-led digital session before hands-on practice
constraints: Students remained neutral about digital courses replacing hands-on instruction; the article states traditional instruction remains critical for hands-on training
examples: In the RCT, the experimental group received a 90-minute digital course in Week 1 and self-directed 3D model practice in Week 2, then both groups did the same Week 3 hands-on plaster carving session; the experimental group outperformed controls on the carving test.

description: The article treats fidelity as calibratable rather than fixed: "fidelity is not a fixed attribute, but a multidimensional concept that must align with the learner's stage and objectives." It recommends a "blended curriculum using cadavers for fine anatomical dissection and synthetic models for high-risk or rare pathology", enabling coaches to match anatomical realism for juniors and pathology-rich scenario fidelity for seniors.
requirements: Selection flexibility in fidelity levels, as some residents reach training competence milestones quicker than others.

examples: The article proposes cadavers for fine anatomical dissection and synthetic models for high-risk or rare pathology, trading some anatomical accuracy for pathology-rich, complication-driven scenarios

citation: Knöchelmann AC, Becker J-N, Stiller G, Steinmann D, Behrends M. (2025). Digital redesign of the radiotherapy course for medical students with a blended learning approach. Strahlentherapie Und Onkologie. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00066-024-02348-x
title: Blended learning pattern interweaving digital self-learning modules, activating online case seminars, and clinical practical experience

Prepared case studies implemented as digital surveys whose results teachers review before the synchronous discussion
A workshop to align the doctors conducting the seminars on the didactic concept
constraints: Development of the new teaching concept required considerable effort, as the authors themselves note as a criticism
Best suited to subjects where theoretical knowledge must transfer to practical work and decision-making rather than manual skills training
examples: Students worked through an online workflow on radiation preparation and planning, discussed case studies in the video-conference seminar, and physically made an irradiation mask during the block internship.

title: A 40-hour blended simulation-based laparoscopic training program with online and two proficiency-based face-to-face modules
description: The program comprised an online module (10 weekly classes on laparoscopic fundamentals) followed by face-to-face Basic and Endosuture modules totalling 40 hours, 20 hours each. Its design "involved various teaching strategies, feedback, repetition of practice, variation of difficulties, increasing complexity, distributed practice, cognitive interaction, individualization of learning, clinical context variation, and knowledge integration". Face-to-face practice was proficiency-based and progressive: the resident only advanced after reaching the previous exercise's goal, across eight dry-lab exercises.

constraints: Developed and evaluated during COVID-19 confinement; validation studies are needed before large-scale implementation, per the authors

title: Bloom's revised taxonomy as the theoretical basis of the flipped classroom model with pre-class and in-class components
description: The article grounds the flipped classroom model in Bloom's revised taxonomy, which it describes as having six levels of learning "arranged from the lowest level below to the highest level at the top": Remembering, Understanding, Applying, Analyzing, Evaluating, and Creating. Through these levels students recall information, understand concepts, interpret and summarize, apply knowledge, and produce creative thinking. Based on this taxonomy, the article states the FCM had two components, pre-class learning and in-class learning, moving lower-level learning outside class and higher-level application into class activities.
requirements: Pre-class learning materials must be studied by students before class so class time can be used for interaction and application
target_learning_goals: moving recall of facts outside class
focusing class time on understanding, application and higher-order thinking
examples: The study operationalized the two components by giving group A pre-class materials and using class time for iRAT, tRAT, discussion and application exercises

title: Blended learning pattern for rare obstetric emergencies: advance e-learning followed by individual simulation on a birth simulator
description: The article's blended learning concept links an online element with a face-to-face simulation: "participants were provided in advance with approximately one hour of e-learning containing theoretical knowledge about the diagnosis and treatment of shoulder dystocia," after which knowledge was applied on a SimMom birth simulator using the HELPERR scheme. citation: Mello Luciane V, Watson Helen, Smith David P., Francis Nigel J. (2022). Engagement with video content in the blended classroom. Essays in Biochemistry. https://doi.org/10.1042/EBC20210055
title: Blended laboratory preparation: pre-sessional videos, interactive tools and simulations supporting lab work
description: The article describes extending blended learning to laboratory teaching through pre-recorded videos introducing "key laboratory concepts, including health and safety and the use of equipment", embedded in pre-sessional materials. Tools like EdPuzzle embed interactivity with real-time feedback, and simulations generate unique datasets so students can problem-solve in a consequence-free environment before the laboratory session. Innovations have been shared through the #DryLabsRealScience network and the lectureremotly.com website.
requirements: Recorded preparation material is embedded into pre-sessional materials ahead of the physical laboratory session
constraints: What cannot be replaced digitally, however, is the psychomotor skills that are developed through the physical act of laboratory work
target_learners: undergraduate bioscience students preparing for laboratory classes
target_learning_goals: laboratory preparedness, health and safety knowledge, and equipment use

citation: Siebert JN, Glangetas A, Grange M, Haddad K, Courvoisier DS, Lacroix L. (2022). Impact of blended learning on manual defibrillator's use: A simulation‐based randomized trial. Nurs Crit Care. 2022;27(4):501‐511. https://doi.org/10.1111/nicc.12713
title: Adopt blended learning that integrates learner-centred online content with face-to-face instruction to teach manual defibrillator skills in hospitals
description: The article recommends a shift from traditional instructor-led face-to-face classroom teaching to blended learning combining a standardized face-to-face course with a tailored, gamified 20- to 30-minute e-learning course of identical content. It reports that "Proficiently teaching the use of a manual defibrillator can be performed through blended learning" and that blended learning "may be a feasible alternative to face‐to‐face learning for hands‐on manual defibrillator skill acquisition in paediatric emergency departments."
requirements: A 20-minute standardized face-to-face course plus a 20- to 30-minute e-learning course whose content is exactly the same as that taught and tested
constraints: The article cautions that the lack of a significant difference between both educational methods observed at the level of each electrical procedure prompts caution, and that single-session training of either kind did not prevent skill decay at 2 months
target_learners: registered nurses and postgraduate year-1 to year-5 residents in paediatric emergency departments and paediatric intensive care units
target_learning_goals: proficient and correct use of a manual defibrillator for defibrillation, synchronized cardioversion and transcutaneous pacing
examples: Participants allocated to the blended learning arm did the FFL course and immediately after had an additional training with a tailored and gamified 20- to 30-minute e-learning course
